summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per GAO, twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number. Most of the reported use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production; in about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI. Reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies are using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets.

The same GAO review found management gaps. There is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI; OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to them, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data; two inventories included AI uses later determined not to be AI. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The excerpts do not name vendors or show where procurement money concentrates.

No source in this set reports return on investment for government AI. GAO notes that without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data, and that until all requirements are met, agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits.

On the policy side, Stanford HAI reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with frameworks for governance, evaluation, and understanding falling behind and data transparency declining. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives and promotes trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles; in July 2024 the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights describes its work as helping governments increase the impact of public services through empowering teams and harnessing technology, but the excerpt gives no adoption figure.

theworldofai.org tracks 5,953 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan, and reviewed 101 measures across 27 states on September 18, 2026. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors: Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting. The recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state created a new agency to enforce AI law; the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act. A private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. A reader deciding whether to deploy in government should expect a patchwork of state laws, human-in-the-loop duties for health, employment, benefits, and education decisions, and record-keeping obligations, with the attorney general as the most likely enforcer.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page tracks 5,948 artificial intelligence bills across 53 US jurisdictions, with data refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to official bill pages. A review of 101 enacted measures across 27 states, dated September 18, 2026, found that no two states wrote the same law, and only Colorado and Texas passed broad laws covering consequential decisions across sectors. Most other measures target a single setting, such as companion chatbots, political ads, insurance prior authorization, classrooms, or state agencies. The page notes recurring rules: AI may assist but cannot be the sole decider in personal matters like insurance denials, therapy, college instruction, or benefit decisions, and enforcement typically falls to state attorneys general rather than new agencies. A private right to sue appears mainly where one identifiable person is harmed.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
